purpose: Fulvestrant is used to treat certain types of breast cancer in women after menopause. It is used when the cancer is hormone receptor-positive, meaning the cancer cells grow in response to estrogen. It may be used alone or combined with other cancer medicines.
how_it_works: Breast cancer cells sometimes have special proteins called estrogen receptors that act like doors — estrogen enters through these doors and tells the cancer to grow. Fulvestrant works by blocking and destroying these doors so estrogen can no longer get in. Without that signal, the cancer cells lose a key trigger for growth and may slow down or stop growing.
common_side_effects: Injection site pain or soreness (it is given as a shot), hot flashes, nausea, fatigue or tiredness, joint or bone pain, headache, and loss of appetite. Some people also notice mild swelling in the hands or feet.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as fulvestrant can seriously harm an unborn baby — reliable birth control is very important while on this medication and for one year after stopping it. Let your doctor know if you have liver problems, since the dose may need to be adjusted. It can also increase the risk of blood clots, so report any leg pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath right away. Avoid receiving live vaccines during treatment without first checking with your healthcare team.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 500 mg (two separate 250 mg injections, one in each buttock) given once a month. An extra dose is given two weeks after the very first injection to help the medicine reach the right level in your body faster. A nurse or doctor gives the injections in a clinic — you do not inject it yourself at home.
